analysis.one_liner: Bans health insurers from denying coverage or charging more for preexisting conditions.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 18 Democratic cosponsors, never received a committee vote or floor vote and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for health insurers to refuse coverage to people with preexisting conditions, whether they get insurance through an employer or buy it on their own. It would also have required insurers to charge everyone the same price for the same policy and post their prices publicly. The idea later became federal law as part of the 2010 Affordable Care Act, but this bill itself sat in committee and never came to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People with preexisting health conditions — cancer survivors, diabetics, people with heart disease — who could be turned down by insurers or charged unaffordable prices under the rules of 2008. It would also help workers changing jobs, since insurers could no longer use waiting periods to skip covering their existing conditions, and anyone shopping for insurance, who would see every insurer's uniform price posted publicly.

how_it_helps.text: It bans preexisting condition exclusions in all group health plans and all individual insurance policies, amending ERISA, the Internal Revenue Code, and the Public Health Service Act, effective for plan years starting January 1, 2009 [S2][S3].
It forces insurers in the individual market to sell coverage to any eligible person who applies and to bar them from imposing preexisting condition exclusions there too [S2][S3].
It requires every insurer to charge the same premium for the same coverage across a metropolitan area and to openly disclose that price, including on the internet [S2][S3].
It requires insurers to accept every employer that applies for group coverage, not just small employers, and to accept every eligible individual during enrollment [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, which lose the ability to deny coverage to sick applicants, charge sick people more, and keep their pricing secret. The cost of covering sicker enrollees would be spread across all policyholders in the form of premiums averaged over the whole market, since the bill contains no subsidy or mandate to offset that cost.

drawbacks.text: The bill bars insurers from turning away sick applicants but contains no requirement that healthy people buy insurance and no subsidies to help pay premiums. Insurers and some economists argued that guaranteed coverage without a mandate invites people to wait until they get sick to buy a policy, which can drive up premiums for everyone who stays enrolled; the bill's answer is only to let the Health and Human Services Secretary write rules to discourage that behavior [S2][S3].

The guaranteed-issue and uniform-premium rules would apply only to citizens, permanent residents, and other lawfully present immigrants, leaving lawfully present noncitizens covered but others outside the guarantee [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections for people with preexisting conditions were real and substantial — versions of them became law in 2010 and remain popular. The bill's weakness is that it bans discrimination without building the funding side: no mandate, no subsidies, and only a loose instruction to the Secretary to deter people from buying coverage only when sick. That gap was the standard objection to guaranteed-issue bills of this era, and it is why the eventual law paired the ban with a mandate and subsidies. Even with that flaw, the bill's benefits to sick people clearly outweigh its costs to insurers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then to a health subcommittee on the day it was introduced, and none of them ever brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Kagen introduced the bill on February 14, 2008, with 18 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means committees on the day of introduction [S5].
It was then referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and the record shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress [S5].
Bans on preexisting condition exclusions and guaranteed issue in the individual market later became law through the Affordable Care Act of 2010, taking effect in 2014.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept their ability to deny coverage and price by health status through 2014, and the millions of Americans with preexisting conditions went without the protection for another six years.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors were House Democrats, and the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record of how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill removes the core of health underwriting: insurers could no longer deny applicants with preexisting conditions, impose waiting periods, charge sick people more than healthy ones, or keep premiums undisclosed. Insurers profit by pricing and excluding risk, so their interest ran against the bill's guarantee of coverage for sick people.

Group plans, including self-insured ERISA plans, lose the ability to impose preexisting condition exclusions on new hires, which raises plan costs for employers with turnover. Workers gain immediate coverage when they change jobs.

industries.industry: Insurance agents and brokers selling individual policies
industries.note: Guaranteed issue means insurers must sell to anyone, so brokers lose the underwriting-based product mix but gain a market where every applicant can be enrolled.
